definitions.definition: A structural similarity or mapping between two different systems that preserves their underlying patterns.
definitions.example: Like how a map of a subway system and the actual subway system have the same structure even though one is paper and the other is tunnels and trains.

definitions.definition: The study of how living things interact with each other and their environment.
definitions.example: Scientists studying how wolves, deer, and trees affect each other in a forest.

definitions.definition: The study of the church, its nature, structure, and purpose.
definitions.example: Theologians discussing what the church should look like based on the Bible.

definitions.definition: The variety of different species of plants, animals, and other living things in a particular area.
definitions.example: A rainforest has high biodiversity because it has many different types of trees, birds, insects, and mammals.

definitions.definition: A species that has a very large effect on its environment relative to its abundance, and whose removal causes major changes.
definitions.example: Sea otters are a keystone species because they eat sea urchins, which would otherwise destroy kelp forests.

definitions.definition: Effects that travel down a food chain when a top predator is removed or added, causing changes at every level.
definitions.example: When wolves were removed from Yellowstone, elk overpopulated and ate too many young trees, changing the whole landscape.

definitions.definition: A species that is not native to an area and causes harm to the environment, economy, or human health.
definitions.example: Zebra mussels from Europe have invaded the Great Lakes, clogging pipes and outcompeting native mussels.

definitions.definition: The process by which the structure of a biological community changes over time, from simple to more complex.
definitions.example: A bare rock first gets lichens, then mosses, then grasses, then shrubs, and finally a forest.

definitions.definition: The maximum number of individuals of a species that an environment can support without being damaged.
definitions.example: A pond can only support so many fish before they run out of food and oxygen.

definitions.definition: A relationship between two species where both benefit.
definitions.example: Clownfish live among sea anemones; the clownfish gets protection and the anemone gets cleaned.

definitions.definition: A relationship where one organism benefits at the expense of another.
definitions.example: A tick feeds on a dog's blood, harming the dog while the tick gets food.

definitions.definition: The movement and exchange of nutrients (like carbon, nitrogen) between living things and the environment.
definitions.example: When a leaf falls and rots, its nutrients go back into the soil to feed new plants.

definitions.definition: Changes in population or community structures that occur at the boundary of two habitats.
definitions.example: The edge of a forest next to a field often has more bird species than deep inside the forest.

definitions.definition: The ability of a system to recover from disturbances and keep functioning.
definitions.example: A diverse forest can recover from a storm better than a farm with only one crop.

definitions.definition: The Apostle Paul's teachings about the church, especially its unity and diversity of gifts.
definitions.example: Paul's letters like 1 Corinthians and Ephesians explain how the church should work together like a body.

definitions.definition: A belief or teaching that goes against the official teachings of a religion.
definitions.example: Saying Jesus was not really human was considered heresy by the early church.

definitions.definition: The process of helping others grow in their faith and become more like Jesus.
definitions.example: A mentor meeting weekly with a new believer to study the Bible and pray together.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that measures how many different types of things are in a group and how evenly they are distributed.
definitions.example: Scientists use it to compare the biodiversity of two forests: one with many equally common species scores higher than one dominated by a single species.

definitions.definition: A part or share of a whole, often written as a fraction or decimal.
definitions.example: If 3 out of 10 students are left-handed, the proportion of left-handed students is 0.3.

definitions.definition: A pattern showing that larger areas tend to contain more species.
definitions.example: A large island usually has more types of birds than a small island nearby.

definitions.definition: A relationship where one quantity changes as a power of another, often producing a straight line on a log-log graph.
definitions.example: The number of species on an island increases roughly as the island's area raised to the 0.25 power.

definitions.definition: When two things tend to change together, either in the same or opposite direction.
definitions.example: Ice cream sales and temperature are correlated: when it's hotter, more ice cream is sold.

definitions.definition: Growing only one type of plant or having only one type of thing in a system.
definitions.example: A cornfield that has only corn is a monoculture, unlike a meadow with many wildflowers.

definitions.definition: A failure in a system that spreads from one part to others, causing a chain reaction of breakdowns.
definitions.example: When a power line goes down, it can overload other lines and cause a blackout across a whole region.

definitions.definition: The gradual weakening or loss of correct religious teachings over time.
definitions.example: If a church stops teaching that Jesus rose from the dead, that's doctrinal erosion.

definitions.definition: When a group breaks apart into smaller, disconnected pieces.
definitions.example: A church splitting into two groups that no longer talk to each other.

definitions.definition: Teaching that is healthy, correct, and based on the Bible.
definitions.example: A pastor explaining what the Bible really says about forgiveness is sound teaching.

definitions.definition: Ecological succession that starts on bare rock or sand with no soil.
definitions.example: After a volcano erupts and covers land with lava, plants slowly grow from scratch.

definitions.definition: The first species to colonize a barren area, making it easier for later species to move in.
definitions.example: Lichens are pioneer species that grow on bare rock and help create soil.

definitions.definition: The final, stable stage of ecological succession, with a diverse and balanced set of species.
definitions.example: An old-growth forest with many tree species, ferns, and animals is a climax community.

definitions.definition: A suggested limit of about 150 people that a person can maintain stable social relationships with.
definitions.example: You might know 500 people on social media, but you can only really keep up with about 150.

definitions.definition: The limit of how many relationships a person's brain can manage at once.
definitions.example: Your brain can only keep track of so many friends' names, faces, and stories before it gets overwhelmed.

definitions.definition: How many close, meaningful relationships exist within a group relative to its size.
definitions.example: A small church where everyone knows each other well has high relational density.

definitions.definition: A very large church, typically with thousands of members.
definitions.example: A church that meets in a huge auditorium and has multiple services each weekend.

definitions.definition: Leadership that uses followers for the leader's own benefit rather than serving them.
definitions.example: A pastor who demands high salaries and fancy cars while the congregation struggles.

definitions.definition: A leadership style where the leader focuses on serving and empowering others.
definitions.example: A manager who helps their team succeed rather than bossing them around.

definitions.definition: A transition zone between two different ecosystems, often rich in species.
definitions.example: The area where a forest meets a grassland is an ecotone with plants and animals from both habitats.

definitions.definition: The study of how to spread a religion, especially Christianity, across cultures.
definitions.example: Scholars studying why some missionary efforts succeed while others fail.

definitions.definition: Having multiple species or parts that can perform the same role, so if one fails, another can take over.
definitions.example: In a forest, several different bird species eat the same insects, so losing one bird doesn't cause insect overpopulation.

definitions.definition: Teaching that agrees with the accepted, traditional beliefs of a religion.
definitions.example: The belief that Jesus is both fully God and fully human is orthodox Christian teaching.

definitions.definition: Mixing different religious beliefs together, often in a way that changes the original teachings.
definitions.example: Combining Christian beliefs with local spirit worship so that both are practiced together.

definitions.definition: A mapping between two systems that preserves their structure, even if the systems are made of different things.
definitions.example: The way a family tree and a company's org chart both show who reports to whom, even though one is about relatives and the other about jobs.

definitions.definition: A measure of how deeply a concept changes the way we think about something, from surface to deep structure.
definitions.example: Saying 'the church is like a body' is a surface reframe; showing it follows the same rules as ecosystems is a deeper reframe.

definitions.definition: A statement that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; in simple terms, things tend to get messier over time.
definitions.example: Your bedroom naturally gets messier if you never clean it — that's entropy increasing.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation — how people are saved from sin and its consequences.
definitions.example: Christians believe salvation comes through faith in Jesus, but different groups have different views on exactly how that works.

definitions.definition: How diseases or ideas spread through a population, including factors like transmission rate and immunity.
definitions.example: How a flu virus moves from one person to another in a school, or how a rumor spreads through a town.
